title: Alan Freed and rock and roll displace big-band jazz
summary: McRae says Freed's rock and roll made it hard for jazz records, and he recalls Stanley Turrentine recording "Broadway".

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well you got to take things -- you take things in area. Like (inaudible) the type the Fats Domino area, you know.
This will give you an idea what really happened to big bands. When Alan Freed came in -- this was the killing of a lot of things -- a lot of styles and things.
These things came in -- they were so big and popular, that a lot of people forgot -- If you didn't have a big jazz record on the market, you couldn't break through.
Stanley Turrentine, he came up from the Minton Playhouse, you know. He was doing a lot of things (inaudible) -- on Columbia.
He did for me on Blue Note "Broadway" on two or three different records. He did Broadway twice (inaudible) Minton Playhouse.
Did it once with his own group, and did it once with the girl he was married to on organ.
